title: Stage 3: Creating tasks
summary: Accept new tasks with POST, validate them, and answer 201 Created with a Location header.

steps.title: POST and the request body
body: Reading is half an API. This stage lets clients **create** tasks.
Creating is the job of `POST`. A client sends `POST /tasks`, which reads as *add this to the tasks collection*, and puts the new task in the **request body** as JSON:
`Content-Type` is a **header**: a named piece of information about the request. This one tells the server how to read the body.
The client does not send an id. The server owns the ids, so it picks one.
Describe the JSON you expect with a record, and take it as a parameter:
ASP.NET Core reads the body, parses the JSON, and builds the record for you. JSON `text` fills the property `Text`: matching ignores case.
`Text` is `string?` on purpose. Nothing stops a client from sending `{}`, and then the property is `null`. Input from outside is never guaranteed, and the type should say so.
`POST` is neither safe nor repeatable: send the same POST twice and you get two tasks.

steps.prompt: A client talks to the Tasks API. Where does each piece of information travel?
items: The id of the task to read
The title of a task being created
A long description for a new task
steps.explain: The URL says *which* resource. The body carries the *content* you are sending. Headers carry information *about* the request or response.

steps.title: 201 Created and Location
body: A successful POST could answer `200 OK`, but HTTP has a more exact code: **`201 Created`**. It tells the client that a new resource now exists.
Since the server chose the id, the client needs to learn it. A good `201` response does that twice:
- The **`Location` header** holds the URL of the new resource.
- The **body** is the resource as the server stored it, so the client does not need a second request to see it.
One helper does all three things:
The first argument becomes the `Location` header. The second becomes the JSON body.
One more than the highest id in use. An empty list has no highest, so that case starts at 1:

steps.explain: The next id comes from the highest one in use (5), not from the count (3). Counting would hand out id 4 here and, with other data, an id that is already taken. `Max()` on an empty list throws, which is why the empty case is handled first.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into an endpoint that creates a note and answers `201 Created`.
steps.explain: Work out the id, build the note, store it, then report it. The id must be computed before the note is added, or `Max` would see the new note.

steps.title: Create a task
prompt: - Bind the body to a record `CreateTask(string? Title)`.
- The new task's id is one more than the highest id in the list. With the three starting tasks, the first one created gets id 4 and the next gets id 5.
- A new task is never done: `done` is `false`.
- Add the task to the list, so `GET /tasks` and `GET /tasks/4` can see it.
- Respond `201 Created`, with a `Location` header of `/tasks/{id}` and the created task as the body.
Assume the title is sensible for now. The next step deals with bad input.
starter: return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);
solution: return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
var task = new TaskItem(id, request.Title ?? "", false);

static class DojoTests
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The earlier endpoints could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /health still returns ok", "ok", await DojoWeb.Text(await http.GetAsync("/health")));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks still starts with tasks 1, 2 and 3", "1,2,3", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks/2 still returns \"Build an API\"", "Build an API", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync("/tasks/2")), "title"));
DojoWeb.Status("GET /tasks/99 still responds 404 Not Found", 404, await http.GetAsync("/tasks/99"));
await Dojo.TryAsync("POST /tasks could be checked", async () =>
var r = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/tasks", new { title = "Write tests" });
DojoWeb.Status("POST /tasks with a title responds 201 Created", 201, r);
var location = r.Headers.Location?.ToString();
Dojo.Check("the response has the header Location: /tasks/4", location is not null && location.EndsWith("/tasks/4"), "the Location header was " + (location ?? "missing"));
var json = await DojoWeb.Json(r);
Dojo.Eq("the body is the created task, with id 4", "4", DojoWeb.Prop(json, "id"));
Dojo.Eq("the created task has the title that was sent", "Write tests", DojoWeb.Prop(json, "title"));
Dojo.Eq("the created task is not done", "false", DojoWeb.Prop(json, "done"));
var fetched = await http.GetAsync("/tasks/4");
DojoWeb.Status("GET /tasks/4 then responds 200 OK", 200, fetched);
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks/4 returns the new task", "Write tests", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(fetched), "title"));
var second = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/tasks", new { title = "Deploy" });
DojoWeb.Status("a second POST /tasks responds 201 Created", 201, second);
Dojo.Eq("the second created task gets id 5", "5", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(second), "id"));
var location2 = second.Headers.Location?.ToString();
Dojo.Check("its Location header is /tasks/5", location2 is not null && location2.EndsWith("/tasks/5"), "the Location header was " + (location2 ?? "missing"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks now lists tasks 1 to 5", "1,2,3,4,5", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks"));
// "1,2,3" for a JSON array of tasks, so one row can check which tasks came back and in what order.
static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array
? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, "id")))
: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));

steps.title: Validation and 400 Bad Request
body: Your endpoint currently stores whatever arrives: an empty title, a missing title, a title of ten thousand characters. A public API must check its input, because sooner or later someone sends every wrong thing possible.
When the request itself is at fault, the answer is **`400 Bad Request`**, and nothing is stored. A bare 400 leaves the caller guessing, so send a small JSON body that explains:
Pick one shape for errors and use it everywhere. Clients can then handle every failure with the same code. This project uses `{"error":"..."}`.
## A helper keeps the rules in one place
It returns the problem, or `null` when there is none. Stage 4 will need the same rules again, so a helper saves you from copying them.
> **Tip:** If the body is not JSON at all, your handler never runs. ASP.NET Core cannot build the record, so it answers 400 by itself.

steps.prompt: Which status code should each response carry?
steps.explain: An empty list is still a successful answer: `200 OK` with `[]`. 404 means the URL names nothing, and the collection `/tasks` always exists. 400 means the request was understood and found faulty.

steps.prompt: Each title is checked the way your endpoint will check it. What does this print?
steps.explain: `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is true for `null`, for the empty string, and for a string of only spaces. One call covers all three kinds of blank.

steps.title: Reject bad titles
prompt: Make `POST /tasks` validate the title before it stores anything.
A title is **invalid** when it is
- longer than 100 characters. Exactly 100 is fine.
For an invalid title, respond `400 Bad Request` with a JSON body that has an `error` property holding a message for the caller. The wording is yours.
A rejected request must not add a task and must not use up an id.
A valid request behaves as before: `201 Created`, the `Location` header, and the task as the body.
starter: return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
var task = new TaskItem(id, request.Title ?? "", false);

solution: return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
if (error is not null) return Results.BadRequest(new { error });
var task = new TaskItem(id, request.Title!, false);
if (title.Length > 100) return "Title must be 100 characters or fewer.";
record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);

hints: Check the title at the top of the handler and return early. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.Title)` covers null, empty and spaces. `request.Title.Length > 100` covers the rest.
`return Results.BadRequest(new { error = "Title is required." });` sends status 400 with the body `{"error":"Title is required."}`.

A helper `string? ValidateTitle(string? title)` that returns a message or `null` keeps the handler short: `var error = ValidateTitle(request.Title); if (error is not null) return Results.BadRequest(new { error });`. After that check the title cannot be null, and `request.Title!` tells the compiler so.
